items.name: Hold
items.definition: Any shaped grip bolted to the wall for hands or feet.
items.kid: The bumps on the wall you grab or stand on.
items.demo: Touch three holds and name their colors.
items.explanation: A climbing hold is a shaped grip, usually bolted to a wall, that you grab or stand on. Holds are arranged in paths called routes by route setters, and they come in many shapes (jugs, crimps, pinches, slopers, volumes).
items.whyItMatters: Naming hold types helps kids choose feet and hands on purpose, and it is the language of route reading.
items.howToCoachIt: Touch and name a jug, a crimp, a pinch, a sloper, and a foothold on the wall in front of you. Momentum's Mo Mini list starts with those basic names.

items.name: Jug
items.definition: A large, deep, positive hold that is easy to grip.
items.kid: A big hold shaped like a jug handle.
items.demo: Hang from a jug and from a small hold; compare.
items.explanation: A jug (also called a bucket in the glossary) is a large handhold that is very easy to use.
items.whyItMatters: Jugs are the right place to teach new movement, rests, and straight arms, because the hands can hold on while the feet and hips learn the skill.
items.howToCoachIt: Ask the group to find three jugs and then do a drill (hover feet, robot arms, or a mantle press) only on those large holds first.

items.name: Crimp
items.definition: A small, thin edge held with the fingertips; also the grip used on it.
items.kid: A tiny ledge you hold with your fingertips.
items.demo: Show open-hand and half-crimp on a big edge; no full crimp for young kids.

items.name: Sloper
items.definition: A rounded hold with no edge; it relies on friction and body position.
items.kid: A round, smooth hold you hug with your whole hand.
items.demo: Hold it with straight arms and hips low and pulled in high.

items.name: Pinch
items.definition: A hold squeezed between thumb and fingers.
items.kid: A hold you pinch like a crab claw.
items.demo: Squeeze a pinch with and without the thumb.

items.name: Pocket
items.definition: A hole in a hold for one or more fingers (one-finger pockets, monos, are not for youth).
items.kid: A hole you poke fingers into.
items.demo: Count how many fingers fit.

items.name: Sidepull
items.definition: A hold facing sideways, pulled toward the body's midline.
items.kid: A hold you pull sideways, like opening a sliding door.
items.demo: Lean away from a sidepull to make it work.

items.name: Undercling
items.definition: A hold facing down, gripped palm-up with feet high.
items.kid: A hold you grab from underneath, like lifting a box.
items.demo: Grip palm-up and walk feet higher.

items.name: Gaston
items.definition: A hold pushed outward with the elbow out, thumb down.
items.kid: A hold you push open, like opening elevator doors.
items.demo: Mime opening elevator doors, then on the wall.

items.name: Volume
items.definition: A large hollow feature bolted to the wall, often with holds on it.
items.kid: A giant shape on the wall you can stand or grab on.
items.demo: Climb onto a volume and stand on it.

items.name: Foothold
items.definition: A hold used for feet; small ones are called chips or jibs.
items.kid: A hold for your feet.
items.demo: Find the smallest foothold in reach.
items.explanation: A foothold is any place you stand: a bolt-on hold, a chip, a volume, or a smear on the wall itself. Wikipedia's glossary treats a hold as a place to cling, grip, jam, press, or stand.
items.whyItMatters: Looking at the foothold before you place the foot is the shared idea behind quiet feet, sticky feet, hover feet, and downclimbing.
items.howToCoachIt: Ask the climber to point to the next foothold, then watch whether the foot lands there quietly and stays.

items.name: Hold Direction
items.definition: Which way a hold's best surface faces; it decides how to pull. Positive holds are incut; negative ones slope away.
items.kid: Which way the hold's grab side points.
items.demo: Find the 'smile' of a hold before grabbing.

items.name: Smear
items.definition: Pressing the sole flat on the wall with no foothold, using friction.
items.kid: Pressing your shoe flat on the wall to stick.
items.demo: Walk feet up blank wall while holding a jug.
items.explanation: Smearing is using friction from the sole of the climbing shoe when there are no good footholds to stand on. It is a central skill of slab climbing, which emphasizes balance, footwork, and smearing on walls that are less than vertical.
items.whyItMatters: If kids only hunt for edges, they miss a lot of useful feet, especially on slab.
items.howToCoachIt: Start on a low-angle slab. Weight the whole sole and keep the hip over the foot. Contrast it with edging on a nearby narrow foothold.

images.alt: Close view of a climbing shoe smearing on rock, the sole pressed flat to use friction.
Climber standing on a friction slab with weight over smeared feet.

sources.title: Glossary: smearing, edging, slab, slab climbing

items.name: Edging
items.definition: Standing on a hold with the inside or outside edge of the shoe.
items.kid: Standing on the side of your shoe.
items.demo: Inside edge, then outside edge, on the same hold.
items.explanation: Edging uses the edge of the climbing shoe on a narrow foothold. When there is no foothold to edge on, smearing (friction from the sole) is used instead.
items.whyItMatters: Choosing an edge or a smear is basic footwork. Precise placement still matters for both.
items.howToCoachIt: Find a small edge and a blank patch of wall side by side. Have the climber edge one foot and smear the other, looking at each placement first. No accurate close-up edging photo was available for this draft, so demo on the wall.

items.name: Toeing In
items.definition: Pulling with the toes to keep feet on steep terrain.
items.kid: Pulling the hold toward you with your toes.
items.demo: See Drag a Hold.

items.name: Heel Hook
items.definition: Placing the heel on a hold and pulling with the hamstring.
items.kid: Hooking your heel on a hold like a hand.
items.demo: Heel hook a big hold at waist height.
items.explanation: A heel hook uses the back of the heel to apply pressure on a hold for balance or leverage. It is different from a toe hook, which presses the top of the toes under a hold to pull the body in.
items.whyItMatters: A good heel hook can take weight off the hands and help the hips stay close, especially on steep terrain or a traverse.
items.howToCoachIt: Start with a large, obvious heel on a volume or rail at a comfortable height. Set the heel, then move the hips, then move a hand. Keep pads closed underneath.

images.alt: Indoor heel hook with the back of the heel set on a hold, body and free leg visible.

items.name: Toe Hook
items.definition: Hooking the top of the toes behind a hold.
items.kid: Hooking the top of your toes on a hold.
items.demo: Toe hook a volume edge.

items.name: Foot Swap
items.definition: Replacing one foot with the other on the same hold.
items.kid: Swapping feet on one hold.
items.demo: See Foot Switching.

items.name: Frontstep
items.definition: Standing on the inside edge, hips square to the wall.
items.kid: Standing facing the wall on your big toe side.
items.demo: See Quick Step.

items.name: Backstep
items.definition: Standing on the outside edge with the hip turned in.
items.kid: Standing on your pinky-toe side, hip turned to the wall.
items.demo: See Quick Step.

items.name: High Step
items.definition: Placing a foot high, near the hip or hand.
items.kid: A big step way up high.
items.demo: High step and stand up.
items.explanation: A high step is placing a foot on a hold that is significantly higher than usual, often near the hips or hands, then weighting it to stand up. Momentum groups high steps with toe placement and body position: sometimes the body is stretched, sometimes scrunched, and both can be useful.
items.whyItMatters: Kids often avoid a high foot and over-reach with the hands. A committed high step can make the next hand easy.
items.howToCoachIt: On a vertical wall with large holds, ask for a high foot, eyes on the hold, then a stand-up with hips over that foot. High/Low Feet (10–20 min in Momentum's contact drills) contrasts scrunched feet with a stretched, tip-toe position.

images.alt: Climber making a high step on a boulder, one foot raised high while the body stays close to the wall.

items.name: Rock Over
items.definition: Shifting weight over a high foot to stand on it.
items.kid: Moving your body over a high foot and standing up.
items.demo: See Skipping Holds.

items.name: Quiet Feet
items.definition: Placing feet without noise, which signals precision.
items.kid: Putting your feet down so quietly nobody hears.
items.demo: See Silent Feet.
items.explanation: Quiet feet means placing each foot without noise, which is a signal of a precise, controlled placement. Gresham treats precise footwork as a generic drill: not which kind of placement (edge or smear), but how quietly and carefully the foot is set.
items.whyItMatters: Noisy, slapping feet usually mean the climber did not look and is not standing on the foot with confidence.
items.howToCoachIt: Momentum's Quiet Sticky Ninja Feet drill (5–10 min): look at the hold first, place a silent, firm foot, and stand up on it. Do this on easy traverses or routes. Do not turn missed silence into an elimination game.

sources.title: Neil Gresham: Improve Your Movement — precise footwork

items.name: Drop Knee
items.definition: Turning one knee down and in to bring the hip to the wall.
items.kid: Twisting your knee down so your hip touches the wall.
items.demo: Drop knee on two footholds at the same height.

items.name: Flagging
items.definition: Placing a leg against the wall without a hold to balance.
items.kid: Sticking a leg out like a tail to keep balance.
items.demo: See Monkey Tails.
items.explanation: Flagging is holding a leg in a position to keep balance, rather than to support weight, often to prevent a barn-door swing. The glossary names three types: a normal flag (free foot stays on the same side), a reverse inside-flag (crosses in front of the standing foot), and a reverse outside-flag (crosses behind). A back-step uses the outside (little-toe) edge of the shoe and often appears with a flag.
items.whyItMatters: When both feet are on the same side of the hands, the body can swing. A flag is the usual fix.
items.howToCoachIt: Build a simple problem where both footholds sit on one side. Let the climber feel the barn-door, then add a flag or a taped box for the free leg. Flag Boxes is the matching drill.

images.alt: Climber in a back-step with the free leg flagged to the side for balance.

items.name: Straight Arms
items.definition: Hanging on extended arms so the skeleton holds weight.
items.kid: Hanging like a monkey with long arms.
items.demo: See Robot Arms.
items.explanation: Straight arms means hanging on extended arms so the skeleton, not bent elbows, holds the weight. Gresham: on steep walls the instinct is to straighten the legs and bend the arms when pumped or scared; the better position is arms as straight as possible, shoulders engaged, hips centred below, legs bent.
items.whyItMatters: Bent-arm hanging tires the pumps quickly. Straight arms are one of Gresham's generic movement drills, alongside precise feet.
items.howToCoachIt: On an easy steep climb, use Robot Arms and Gresham's loop: precise feet, straight arms, relaxed grip. Do not use a hard project for the first look at this cue.

sources.title: Neil Gresham: Improve Your Movement — straight arms, relaxed grip

items.name: Lock-Off
items.definition: Holding a bent arm still while the other hand reaches.
items.kid: Freezing one arm bent while you reach.
items.demo: See Hover Hands.

items.name: Dyno
items.definition: A jump where the body leaves contact to catch a hold.
items.kid: A jump to a hold.
items.demo: See Dyno Dash.
items.explanation: A dyno is a dynamic jump or leap to an out-of-reach hold; missing the hold will usually result in a fall. A deadpoint is a more controlled dynamic in which the hold is grabbed at the apex of the movement while other points of contact remain.
items.whyItMatters: Dynos are exciting and easy to overuse. They belong on closed pads or a belay, at a height you have agreed, after the climber can do the same wall statically when the holds allow it.
items.howToCoachIt: Compare a static reach and a short padded dyno to a large hold. Talk about the landing before the first jump.

images.alt: Climber on a boulder making a dynamic reach, one foot off, both hands going to a higher hold.

items.name: Deadpoint
items.definition: A dynamic move catching a hold at the top of the body's movement.
items.kid: A quick reach at the floaty moment.
items.demo: Deadpoint on a big hold.

items.name: Static
items.definition: Slow, controlled movement keeping three points on.
items.kid: Moving slow and smooth like a sloth.
items.demo: See Static and Dynamic.
items.explanation: In this program, static means slow, controlled movement that keeps three points of contact. It is the opposite of a dyno (a jump to an out-of-reach hold). A deadpoint sits in between: a controlled dynamic where the hand arrives at the apex while the other contacts stay on.
items.whyItMatters: Kids often jump when a static move would work. Teaching both words lets them choose the movement the hold actually needs.
items.howToCoachIt: Do the same easy sequence once statically, then ask whether any reach truly needs a jump. Save committed dynos for padded, agreed tries.

items.name: Dynamic
items.definition: Movement using momentum.
items.kid: Moving fast with a swing or jump.
items.demo: See Static and Dynamic.

items.name: Match
items.definition: Putting both hands (or feet) on the same hold.
items.kid: Both hands on one hold.
items.demo: Match on a jug.
items.explanation: In this program, a match is putting both hands, or both feet, on the same hold. The glossary also mentions a shadow match, which is a quick hand switch on a hold that only fits one hand; that is a more advanced variant, not the basic class meaning.
items.whyItMatters: Matching is a common way to reorganize for the next reach, and it appears in mantles (hand-foot match) as well as on jugs.
items.howToCoachIt: Start on a jug large enough for two hands. Then try a hand-foot match on a low ledge as part of mantle practice.

items.name: Bump
items.definition: Moving one hand twice in a row to reach a better hold.
items.kid: Moving the same hand again.
items.demo: See Systems Wall Drills.

items.name: Cross Through
items.definition: Reaching one hand over or under the other.
items.kid: Crossing your arms to reach.
items.demo: Cross through on a traverse.

items.name: Mantle
items.definition: Pressing down on a ledge to climb on top of it.
items.kid: Pushing down like getting out of a pool.
items.demo: Mantle a volume.

items.name: Layback
items.definition: Pulling on a side edge while pushing feet the opposite way.
items.kid: Pulling and pushing opposite ways on an edge.
items.demo: Layback an arete.
items.explanation: Laybacking (also liebacking) is climbing an edge by side-pulling with both hands and using opposing friction with the feet.
items.whyItMatters: It is a clear example of opposition: hands pull, feet push. It shows up on aretes, crack edges, and some volumes.
items.howToCoachIt: Find a vertical edge or volume rail. Cue pull with the hands, push with the feet, and keep the hips close. Use a height they can downclimb or drop from with pads.

images.alt: Climber laybacking a crack: both hands side-pulling the edge, feet pushing in opposition on the face.

items.name: Stemming
items.definition: Pushing feet and hands against opposing walls.
items.kid: Pushing out on both sides of a corner.
items.demo: Stem in a corner.
items.explanation: Stemming (also called bridging) is climbing opposing walls or a corner by pushing in opposite directions with the feet and hands. Chimneying is the related skill of climbing a cleft large enough for the body.
items.whyItMatters: Opposition can take weight off the arms and even allow a rest. It is also a clear way to feel body tension.
items.howToCoachIt: Use a wide dihedral or two facing volumes. Cue press the feet out. A brief, solid no-hands pause is a useful test on easy stems only.

images.alt: Classic stem / bridge in a wide chimney-like corner, both legs pressing outward.
Climber stemming in an open-book dihedral, feet on opposite walls.

items.name: Knee Bar
items.definition: Wedging the knee and foot between holds to rest.
items.kid: Wedging your knee to rest your arms.
items.demo: Find a knee bar on a volume.

items.name: Cut Feet
items.definition: Feet coming off the wall, usually on steep terrain.
items.kid: When your feet swing off the wall.
items.demo: Show controlled foot return.

items.name: Center of Gravity
items.definition: The body's balance point; climbers keep it over the feet.
items.kid: Your body's balance spot, near your belly button.
items.demo: Stand on one foot and lean.
items.explanation: The centre of gravity is the body's balance point. In this program, climbers learn to keep it over the feet. Gresham's steep-wall position puts the hips centred directly below straight, engaged arms, with the legs bent. A drop-knee is an advanced way to twist the hips — and the centre of gravity — closer to a steep wall.
items.whyItMatters: When the hips drift away from the wall or off the standing foot, feet smear off and arms take the weight.
items.howToCoachIt: On a smear or a hover-feet drill, ask the climber to move the hips over the standing foot. Blok Sessions uses the same cue when a hover starts to swing.

images.alt: Climber on a friction slab with the weight and hips over smeared feet, a clear example of balance over the feet.

sources.title: Neil Gresham: Improve Your Movement — hips centred
Glossary: drop knee (hips and centre of gravity closer to the wall)

items.name: Hips to the Wall
items.definition: Bringing hips close to the wall to shift weight onto feet.
items.kid: Pull your belly or hip toward the wall.
items.demo: Compare hips out and in.

items.name: Three Points of Contact
items.definition: Keeping three limbs on while one moves.
items.kid: Three on, one moves.
items.demo: Count limbs on the wall each move.

items.name: Body Tension
items.definition: Engaging the core to keep feet on and body controlled.
items.kid: Squeezing your middle so you stay stuck.
items.demo: See Keep the Tension.
items.explanation: Body tension is the core and opposing limbs working together so the feet stay on and the body does not sag or swing. Stemming (pressing in opposite directions) and, on steeper ground, a drop-knee are common ways coaches see that tension.
items.whyItMatters: Without tension, even good handholds are not enough on a steep wall or a wide stem; the feet peel and the arms take all the load.
items.howToCoachIt: Use a wide, large-hold stem and ask the climber to press the feet out. On an overhang, Momentum's drop-knee page notes the climber needs both feet outside the centerline and should be cautious of knee strain; keep repetition limited and warm up the lower body.

images.alt: Climber keeping tension by stemming: both legs press outward in a wide corner so the body stays in the wall.

items.name: Turning In
items.definition: Rotating the hips so one side faces the wall, adding reach.
items.kid: Twisting your hip to the wall to reach higher.
items.demo: See Pivot Practice.

items.name: Rest Position
items.definition: A low-effort stance on the wall to recover, often with straight arms, shaking out each hand.
items.kid: A comfy spot on the wall to rest your arms.
items.demo: See Freeze Traverse.

items.name: Harness
items.definition: Waist belt and leg loops that connect a climber to the rope.
items.kid: The seat you wear to tie into the rope.
items.demo: See Harness Check.
items.explanation: A climbing harness is a sewn, load-bearing waist-and-leg device that the rope and other load-bearing gear attach to. On a standard sit harness the rope is tied through the two tie-in points (bridges). The belay loop is for a belay device or an auto-belay connector, attached with a locking carabiner. Gear loops are for racking only. The usual tie-in knot is the figure-eight follow-through, often backed up by a stopper knot. Always check the knot before climbing.
items.whyItMatters: A waist belt worn too low, a knot through the wrong point, or an unlocked locker is a serious error; the partner check exists to catch it every time.
items.howToCoachIt: Lay the harness out, name waist, legs, belay loop, tie-in points, and gear loops, then put it on and check each other. Petzl: “Tie in to the two tie-in points.” For auto belays, staff permission is required, and TRUBLUE says to clip the belay loop only, not multiple hard points.

items.name: Belay Loop
items.definition: The strong loop on a harness for the belay device.
items.kid: The strongest loop on the front of your harness.
items.demo: Point to it on a harness.

items.name: Tie-In Points
items.definition: The two harness points the rope goes through to tie in.
items.kid: The two loops your rope goes through.
items.demo: Thread a rope through both.

items.name: Climbing Shoes
items.definition: Snug, sticky rubber shoes for climbing.
items.kid: Special sticky shoes.
items.demo: Feel the rubber.

items.name: Chalk
items.definition: Magnesium carbonate that dries hands; worn in a bag on the waist.
items.kid: Powder that dries your hands.
items.demo: Chalk up properly.

items.name: Carabiner
items.definition: A metal clip with a gate; lockers have a sleeve that closes the gate.
items.kid: A metal clip; lockers screw shut.
items.demo: Lock and unlock.

items.name: Belay Device
items.definition: A device that adds friction so the belayer can hold and lower the climber.
items.kid: The tool that helps the belayer hold the rope.
items.demo: Show the brake position.

items.name: Quickdraw
items.definition: Two carabiners joined by a sling, used to clip the rope to bolts when leading.
items.kid: Two clips on a strap for lead climbing.
items.demo: See Ground Clipping Practice.

items.name: Crash Pad
items.definition: Foam padding below boulders to reduce landing impact.
items.kid: The squishy floor that cushions falls.
items.demo: See Fall Zones Tour.
items.explanation: A crash pad (or bouldering mat) is a thick foam pad used for protection when bouldering. Modern pads are often about 8–15 cm (3–6 in) thick, with two or three layers of foam in a tough cover; some fold for carrying. They help with repeated short landings on hard or uneven ground, and they are also the standard indoor landing surface under bouldering walls.
items.whyItMatters: Pads only help if they cover the actual landing, including the fall zone, with no gaps.
items.howToCoachIt: On the fall-zone tour, have kids point to closed pad coverage and to gaps. Do not stand, stack bags, or film on a pad that is in use.

images.alt: A folded outdoor crash pad (bouldering mat) standing on end, showing its thick foam construction.
Indoor bouldering wall with a row of thick crash pads covering the landing area.

sources.title: Glossary: bouldering mat, crash pad, spotting

items.name: Auto Belay
items.definition: A device at the top of a wall that takes in rope and lowers the climber.
items.kid: A machine that belays you.
items.demo: Clip-in check demo.

items.name: Rope
items.definition: A stretchy dynamic rope that absorbs fall energy.
items.kid: The stretchy rope that catches you.
items.demo: Pull to feel the stretch.

items.name: Figure-8 Follow-Through
items.definition: The standard tie-in knot; finish with a tail.
items.kid: The knot that ties you to the rope.
items.demo: See Spot the Figure 8.
items.explanation: The figure-eight follow-through (figure-eight loop) is the knot commonly used to tie a climbing rope into a harness. Wikipedia calls it the most common harness tie-in knot: strong, relatively easy to tie and to check, though it can be hard to untie after a heavy load. On a standard sit harness the rope passes through both tie-in points and is retraced; Petzl's figures mark a minimum tail of 10 cm / 3.9 in. Always check the knot before starting to climb.
items.whyItMatters: A knot tied through the belay loop, through only one tie-in point, or with a short un-retraced tail is not the standard gym tie-in taught here.
items.howToCoachIt: Teach the sequence from the Petzl figures: form the eight, pass the tail through both tie-in points, retrace, dress, check the tail. Partners check every time.

items.name: Stopper Knot
items.definition: A knot tied in the rope end so it can't pass through the device.
items.kid: A knot at the rope end.
items.demo: Tie on the end of a practice rope.

items.name: Tail
items.definition: The extra rope past a knot.
items.kid: The extra bit of rope left over.
items.demo: Measure a fist-length tail.

items.name: Flaking
items.definition: Running through a rope into a loose pile so it feeds without tangles.
items.kid: Piling the rope so it doesn't tangle.
items.demo: See Flake and Coil.

items.name: Anchor
items.definition: The fixed point the rope runs through at the top.
items.kid: The strong point at the top.
items.demo: Point to the anchors.

items.name: Top Rope
items.definition: Climbing with the rope already running through an anchor above.
items.kid: Climbing with the rope already at the top.
items.demo: Trace the rope from climber to anchor to belayer.

items.name: Lead Climbing
items.definition: Climbing with the rope from below, clipping quickdraws on the way; falls are longer.
items.kid: Bringing the rope up with you and clipping it as you go.
items.demo: See Mock Lead.

items.name: Back-Clip
items.definition: Clipping a quickdraw so the rope runs from the wall side out toward the climber the wrong way, which can unclip in a fall.
items.kid: Clipping the rope in backward.
items.demo: See What Is Wrong?

items.name: Z-Clip
items.definition: Clipping rope from below the previous draw into the next, creating a Z and heavy drag.
items.kid: Grabbing rope from the wrong spot so it zigzags.
items.demo: Show on a ground clipping board.

items.name: Belay
items.definition: Managing the rope to catch and lower a climber.
items.kid: Holding the rope for your climber.
items.demo: See Ground School Belay.
items.explanation: Belaying is managing the rope so a falling climber is caught and, when needed, lowered. The belayer uses a device on the harness belay loop to increase braking force. Devices may be a simple tube (passive) or a cam-assisted device such as a GRIGRI. In a typical setup the climber is tied in with a figure-eight, the rope runs through the top-rope anchor or through protection, and the belayer holds the brake side of the rope. Petzl's REVERSO notice states that the device does not automatically block the rope; the brake strand is always held. Staff permission is required before anyone uses an auto belay; the connector goes to the belay loop only.
items.whyItMatters: Belaying is a partnership skill. The partner check, the commands, and the brake hand are all part of the same system.
items.howToCoachIt: Ground school first, then a top-rope with a backup as your gym requires. Lead belay belongs only in the 12+ and 14+ groups. Load a GRIGRI using the markings on the device (Petzl section 6). Always hold the brake strand.

items.name: Brake Hand
items.definition: The hand that never leaves the brake strand.
items.kid: The hand that never lets go.
items.demo: Shout 'brake hand!' and freeze to check.

items.name: PBUS
items.definition: A tube-device belay sequence: pull, brake, under, slide.
items.kid: Pull, brake, under, slide.
items.demo: Chant and do it slowly.

items.name: Slack
items.definition: Loose rope; also a call for more rope.
items.kid: Loose rope.
items.demo: Show tight and slack.

items.name: Take
items.definition: A call to pull rope tight and hold the climber.
items.kid: Say 'take' to have your belayer hold you.
items.demo: Sit back on a tight rope at the first bolt.

items.name: On Belay?
items.definition: Start-up commands: 'On belay?' / 'Belay on.' / 'Climbing.' / 'Climb on.'
items.kid: The question-and-answer before you climb.
items.demo: See Climbing Commands Call-and-Response.
items.explanation: “On belay?” is the American command a climber uses when ready to be belayed. The standard reply is “Belay on.” The usual start-up then continues “Climbing.” / “Climb on.” These commands come after the partner check, not instead of it.
items.whyItMatters: Clear, loud commands are how both people know the belay is on before anyone leaves the ground.
items.howToCoachIt: Practice the call-and-response on the ground, then use it on every top-rope. The belayer is looking up and holding the brake side of the rope (Petzl primary position and REVERSO notice: always hold the brake side; a REVERSO does not automatically block).

images.alt: Petzl Access Book: primary belaying position, belayer looking up and holding the brake side of the rope.
images.credit: Diagram: Petzl — ACCESS BOOK #1, booklet pages 6–7, primary belaying position
images.license: Petzl technical figure; hosted for internal coaching use with credit and source link

sources.title: Glossary: on belay, belay on, belay

items.name: Lower
items.definition: Commands for coming down and ending the belay.
items.kid: Coming down; feet out, sit back.
items.demo: See Astronaut Lowering.
items.explanation: To lower (or lower-off) is for the belayer to take the climber's weight on the device and bring them down. In this program, lower also covers the commands for coming down and ending the belay. The climber typically sits back with feet on the wall; the belayer keeps holding the brake side of the rope. This is different from a downclimb, where the climber climbs down under their own movement.
items.whyItMatters: A clean lower needs a ready belayer, a locked locker, and clear commands. It is how most gym top-ropes finish.
items.howToCoachIt: Practice commands first. The belayer holds the brake strand throughout (Petzl: always hold the brake side; a REVERSO does not automatically block). Contrast a lower with a downclimb lap.

images.alt: Top-rope pair: climber on the wall and belayer below, rope running to a top anchor and back — the system used to lower.
Tube-style belay device in use, brake hand on the brake strand of the rope.

items.name: Falling!
items.definition: Warning calls: 'Falling!' for the belayer, 'Rock!' for anything dropped.
items.kid: Shout it to warn people.
items.demo: Practice shouting loud.

items.name: Partner Check
items.definition: Checking each other's harness, knot, device and carabiner before every climb.
items.kid: Checking your buddy's gear before climbing.
items.demo: See Partner Check.
items.explanation: A partner check is each person checking the other's harness, knot, belay device, and locking carabiner before every climb. It includes Petzl's rule to tie in through both tie-in points and always check the knot, and to connect a belay device to the belay loop with a locker that is closed, locked, and loaded on the major axis.
items.whyItMatters: The check is how missed buckles, short tails, and unlocked lockers get caught. It is done every time, including by experienced pairs.
items.howToCoachIt: Use a fixed order (harness, knot, device, locker, commands). Partners point at each item. Coach listens and only prompts if a step is skipped.

images.alt: Sit harness with the parts a partner check names: waist, legs, belay loop, tie-in points.
Finished figure-eight through both tie-in points, tail marked 10 cm / 3.9 inch minimum — a standard knot check.

REVERSO technical notice (device on the belay loop; hold the brake side)

items.name: Soft Catch
items.definition: Letting a little rope give during a lead fall so the climber swings in gently.
items.kid: Making a fall feel gentle.
items.demo: Coach-led lead fall demo.

items.name: Bouldering
items.definition: Climbing short walls without ropes over mats.
items.kid: Climbing low walls with no rope over the mats.
items.demo: Point out the bouldering area.

items.name: Problem
items.definition: A set boulder route.
items.kid: A puzzle route on the boulder.
items.demo: Find a problem's start tag.

items.name: Route
items.definition: A designated path of holds, usually one color.
items.kid: The holds you're allowed to use, all one color.
items.demo: See Climb the Rainbow.
items.explanation: A climbing route is the path a climber follows to the top of a problem, a wall, or a piece of rock. Indoors, holds are usually arranged in marked routes by setters.
items.whyItMatters: Reading a route (which holds, which feet, where to rest) is a skill of its own, practiced in add-on, read-and-point, and observation time.
items.howToCoachIt: Stand on the ground, point hand-foot-hand-foot, then climb the plan. Use easy, well-marked color routes for early practice.

items.name: Start Holds
items.definition: The tagged holds a route starts on.
items.kid: The hold with the tape where you start.
items.demo: Find the start tape.

items.name: Top Out
items.definition: The finish of a problem: matching the last hold or climbing onto the top.
items.kid: The end of the climb.
items.demo: Match the finish hold.
items.explanation: To top out is to finish a climb by going over the top to a standing position. On boulders that often means a mantel: pressing down on the shelf (palms down, like getting out of a pool) until you can stand on it. Momentum notes that mantles can include a palm-down press, a hand-foot match, and leaning in over the feet.
items.whyItMatters: Many indoor problems finish at a last hold, but outdoor boulders and some gym top-outs require this press. It is awkward until it is practiced on a low ledge.
items.howToCoachIt: Start on a low padded ledge or volume. Cue the flip to a palm-down press and a lean over the feet. Agree how they will come down.

images.alt: Climber topping out with a mantle, palms pressing down on the lip to stand onto the shelf.

items.name: Downclimb
items.definition: Climbing back down instead of dropping.
items.kid: Climbing down instead of jumping.
items.demo: See Downclimbing.
items.explanation: To downclimb is to descend by climbing downward, rather than being lowered or rappelling. Momentum's drill stresses eye-to-foot contact: look before you place the foot, and use the legs. On a top-rope, the belayer gives enough slack that the climber is not hanging on the rope.
items.whyItMatters: Downclimbing trains feet, control, and a planned way off a boulder. It also adds easy time on the wall for endurance.
items.howToCoachIt: Climb a vertical or slab route, then climb back down. Coach the belayer's slack. On boulders, agree the downclimb before they leave the ground.

items.name: Fall Zone
items.definition: The area under and around a climber where they might land; keep it clear.
items.kid: The mat space where a climber could fall; stay out.
items.demo: See Fall Zones Tour.
items.explanation: The fall zone is the area under and around a climber where they might land. It should be clear of people, bags, and gaps in the pads. Crash pads are the usual surface in the bouldering fall zone; they work only if they actually cover the landing.
items.whyItMatters: Most avoidable bumps in a youth session happen in a busy fall zone, not on the wall.
items.howToCoachIt: Walk a Fall Zones Tour. One climber (and a spotter, if you are spotting) in a zone at a time. If you include auto belays on the tour, they need staff permission, and the connector clips to the belay loop only.

images.alt: Indoor crash pads covering the landing area under a bouldering wall — the fall zone stays on this surface and stays clear.
Auto belay overview: connector on the belay loop only. Auto-belay use needs staff permission, and the area under the climber still stays clear.
