items.name: Spotting
items.definition: Guiding a falling boulderer's hips and head toward the mat.
items.kid: Helping a climber land on the mat.
items.demo: See Spotting Practice.

items.name: Landing Position
items.definition: Landing on feet with bent knees, then rolling back, arms in.
items.kid: Bend knees, land, roll back like a turtle.
items.demo: See Learn to Fall.
items.explanation: The program landing is: land on the feet with bent knees, then roll back, arms in. Crash pads are thick foam mats that give a more forgiving surface for the repeated short falls of bouldering; they do not replace a planned landing.
items.whyItMatters: Reaching back with straight arms, or landing on a pad gap, is how wrists and necks get hurt. The landing is a skill to practice on purpose (see Learn to Fall).
items.howToCoachIt: Practice from a sit, then a low hang, on a closed pad with a clear fall zone. Do not start from a height the climber has not landed from lower down.

images.alt: Continuous indoor crash pads under a bouldering wall, the surface a climber should land on.

items.name: Send
items.definition: Completing a route from start to finish without falling.
items.kid: Finishing a climb without falling.
items.demo: Celebrate on the Team Send Board.
items.explanation: In the glossary, to send is to free-climb a route from start to finish, whether as an onsight, flash, or redpoint. In class it means completing the agreed climb without falling or weighting the rope.
items.whyItMatters: The word is useful, but it should not become the only goal; process goals and quality repeats matter more for learning.
items.howToCoachIt: Celebrate a send, then ask what the feet or the partner check looked like. Keep send off process-goal cards.

items.name: Flash
items.definition: Sending on the first try with prior beta.
items.kid: Finishing on your first try.
items.demo: See Flash or Fail.

items.name: Onsight
items.definition: Sending on the first try with no beta.
items.kid: First-try send with no hints.
items.demo: Read an onsight route from the ground, then climb it.

items.name: Redpoint
items.definition: Sending after practicing the route.
items.kid: Finishing after practicing it.
items.demo: See Redpoint Tactics.

items.name: Project
items.definition: A route worked over multiple sessions.
items.kid: A hard climb you keep practicing.
items.demo: Pick a project and log tries.
items.explanation: A project is a route or boulder you work over more than one session (or many tries in one session) toward a send. The glossary also uses projecting for that longer attempt.
items.whyItMatters: Projects teach planning, one-change-per-try, and patience. They should still leave room in the session for easy movement quality.
items.howToCoachIt: Pick a project that is a stretch, not a desperate fight. Log what changed. Keep process goals alongside the project.

items.name: Beta
items.definition: Information on how to do a route; unrequested beta is 'spray'.
items.kid: The secret plan for a climb.
items.demo: See Beta Swap.

items.name: Crux
items.definition: The hardest move or section.
items.kid: The hardest part.
items.demo: Point to the crux.

items.name: Route Reading
items.definition: Planning a sequence from the ground.
items.kid: Planning your moves before climbing.
items.demo: See Read and Point.

items.name: V-Scale
items.definition: The bouldering difficulty scale, VB/V0 upward.
items.kid: Numbers for how hard a boulder is.
items.demo: See Learn the Grades.

items.name: YDS
items.definition: The North American roped grade scale (5.5, 5.10a…).
items.kid: Numbers for rope climb difficulty.
items.demo: See Guess the Grade.

items.name: Slab
items.definition: Wall less than vertical; balance and footwork terrain.
items.kid: A wall that leans back toward you.
items.demo: See Wall Types.

items.name: Vertical
items.definition: Wall straight up and down.
items.kid: A straight-up wall.
items.demo: See Wall Types.

items.name: Overhang
items.definition: Wall steeper than vertical; a roof is horizontal.
items.kid: A wall that leans over you.
items.demo: See Wall Types.

items.name: Arete
items.definition: An outside corner edge of the wall.
items.kid: The corner edge that sticks out.
items.demo: Layback an arete.

items.name: Dihedral
items.definition: An inside corner.
items.kid: An inside corner like an open book.
items.demo: Stem in it.
items.explanation: A dihedral (an open book) is the inside corner formed where two walls meet; it is the opposite of an arete. Dihedrals are the usual place to teach stemming or bridging.
items.whyItMatters: Kids can often rest or climb more easily in a corner than on a flat wall, if they learn to press out instead of only pulling in.
items.howToCoachIt: Walk the gym and find a corner. Name it, then stem it on large holds. Pair the word with the stemming images.

images.alt: Climber in an open-book dihedral, stemming with feet on the two opposing walls.

items.name: Traverse
items.definition: Climbing sideways near the ground.
items.kid: Climbing sideways.
items.demo: See Freeze Traverse.
items.explanation: A traverse is a section of climbing that moves horizontally rather than straight up. A hand traverse, in the glossary, is a traverse without useful footholds.
items.whyItMatters: Traverses let a whole group share one stretch of wall and are ideal for footwork drills (silent feet, hover feet, add-on) because falls are usually short.
items.howToCoachIt: Set a start and finish at the same height, keep the line within a short step of the mat for the youngest groups, and run one climber per fall zone.

items.name: Warm-Up
items.definition: Raising heart rate and mobility before hard climbing to reduce injury risk.
items.kid: Getting your body ready.
items.demo: See Pulse Raiser.

items.name: Cool-Down
items.definition: Easy movement and stretching after climbing.
items.kid: Slowing down your body at the end.
items.demo: See Cool-Down Stretch & Reflect.

items.name: Pump
items.definition: Forearm fatigue from sustained gripping.
items.kid: When your arms feel tight and tired.
items.demo: Shake out and feel it fade.
items.explanation: Pump (being pumped) is the accumulation of metabolic waste in the forearms so that even a basic grip becomes very hard to hold.
items.whyItMatters: Pump is the usual limit on easy, longer climbing. Straight arms, relaxed grips, and planned rests delay it; fighting a hard move with bent arms brings it on faster.
items.howToCoachIt: On endurance laps, have the athlete notice early pump, shake out, and rest on a jug or a stem. Choose climbs within ability.

sources.title: Neil Gresham: Improve Your Movement — energy and bent arms when pumped

items.name: Endurance
items.definition: The ability to keep climbing a long time.
items.kid: Climbing a long time without getting tired.
items.demo: See Easy Continuous Laps.
items.explanation: Endurance is the ability to keep climbing for longer before the pump takes over. Gresham ties it to efficient movement: graceful, precise climbing conserves energy and lets you climb further on the same effort. Momentum's endurance drills use problems well within ability, not limit projects.
items.whyItMatters: Choosing a hard redpoint to train endurance usually just creates a short, intense fight.
items.howToCoachIt: Easy top-rope laps or linked easy boulders, with one movement cue (straight arms or quiet feet) and planned rests. Downclimbing can add time on the wall if the belayer gives working slack.

sources.title: Neil Gresham: Improve Your Movement — energy conserved

items.name: Power Endurance
items.definition: Repeating hard moves without much rest.
items.kid: Doing hard moves again and again.
items.demo: See Power Endurance Circuits.

items.name: Strength
items.definition: Maximum force for single hard moves.
items.kid: How hard you can pull.
items.demo: See Limit Bouldering.
items.explanation: In this program, strength means maximum force for single hard moves, as distinct from endurance (how long you can keep climbing before the pump). The existing demo is limit bouldering.
items.whyItMatters: Kids often call every hard feeling strength. Separating a single hard move from a long easy pump helps you pick the right drill.
items.howToCoachIt: Use easy, quality movement most of the session. When you do a hard move, keep attempts limited and on large holds for younger groups.

items.name: Mobility
items.definition: Range of motion in hips and shoulders for climbing positions.
items.kid: How far your body can bend.
items.demo: Frog stretch.

items.name: Growth Plate
items.definition: Growing bone ends in kids' fingers; hangboarding and full crimping are deferred for youth to manage injury risk.
items.kid: The growing part of your finger bones that needs care.
items.demo: Show open-hand grip.

items.name: Rest
items.definition: Time off the wall between attempts or sessions.
items.kid: Resting so you can climb strong again.
items.demo: Time a 3-minute rest.

items.name: Training Log
items.definition: A record of climbs, attempts and lessons.
items.kid: A notebook of your climbs.
items.demo: See Goal Setting & Training Log.

items.name: Visualization
items.definition: Mentally rehearsing moves before climbing.
items.kid: Picturing yourself doing the moves.
items.demo: Eyes closed, mime the route.

items.name: Breathing
items.definition: Slow breathing to calm nerves and recover.
items.kid: Slow breaths to calm down.
items.demo: See Belly Breathing.

items.name: Commitment
items.definition: Fully attempting a move once you've decided it is a reasonable risk.
items.kid: Going for the move all the way.
items.demo: See Dyno Dash.

items.name: Fear of Falling
items.definition: Normal fear managed by gradual exposure and practiced falls.
items.kid: Feeling scared to fall, which is normal.
items.demo: See Top-Rope Fall Practice.

items.name: Growth Mindset
items.definition: The belief that ability grows with practice; coaches praise effort and strategy.
items.kid: Your brain grows when you try hard.
items.demo: Praise tries on the Team Send Board.

items.name: Isolation
items.definition: A quiet spot to wait and read before an attempt.
items.kid: The quiet spot where you wait and read.
items.demo: See Pre-Climb Routine.
items.explanation: In this program, isolation is a quiet spot to wait and read before an attempt (see also the pre-climb routine). In competition climbing, an isolation zone is where competitors wait so they do not get beta on upcoming routes. The class meaning is the quieter, closer idea: a place to think before you climb, not the full IFSC isolation procedure.
items.whyItMatters: A short pause to look, away from other people's beta, makes read-and-point and observation time actually work.
items.howToCoachIt: Show the group a waiting spot off the pads. No spraying beta to someone who is in their isolation or observation time unless they ask.

items.name: Observation Period
items.definition: Time set aside to read a route before climbing.
items.kid: Time to look at the route.
items.demo: See Pre-Climb Routine.
items.explanation: Observation period is time set aside to read a route before climbing. In competition it is a formal window; in class it is the same idea as a pre-climb routine: look, point, and plan before you leave the ground. It is related to, but not the same as, competition isolation (waiting away from beta).
items.whyItMatters: A short look from the ground often changes the first sequence and reduces panicked grabbing.
items.howToCoachIt: Give a fixed, quiet minute. Climbers may point but do not start climbing and do not shout beta to someone who is still observing.

items.name: Zone
items.definition: A marked hold partway up a problem.
items.kid: The halfway points hold.
items.demo: Tape a zone on a problem.
items.explanation: In this program a zone is a marked hold partway up a problem (as in competition bouldering, where a zone hold sits between the start and the top). Wikipedia also describes a low zone as a marked intermediate hold used for scoring.
items.whyItMatters: Marking a mid-point hold gives a process target that is not only whether they topped it.
items.howToCoachIt: Tape a zone on an easy problem and celebrate reaching it with control, then the top. Do not confuse this with the fall zone, which is the landing area.

sources.title: Glossary: low zone / zone hold, isolation zone

items.name: Attempt
items.definition: One go at a route.
items.kid: One try.
items.demo: Count your own attempts on one problem.

items.name: Speed Climbing
items.definition: Moving quickly on easy, familiar terrain and comparing the result with your own time.
items.kid: A timed climb you compare with your own best.
items.demo: See Precision Speed.

items.name: Sportsmanship
items.definition: Respecting others: taking turns, cheering, not spraying beta.
items.kid: Being a good teammate and taking turns.
items.demo: Cheer every climber.
items.explanation: In this program, sportsmanship means respecting others: taking turns, cheering, and not spraying beta when a climber wants to work a problem themselves.
items.whyItMatters: Youth sessions share walls and pads; how the group treats a try matters as much as the try.
items.howToCoachIt: Build it into process goals and into three good choices. Cheer every climber, and ask before offering beta.

items.name: Barn Door
items.definition: An uncontrolled swing away from the wall when the points of contact line up on one side; usually fixed with a flag.
items.kid: When your body swings open like a door on a hinge.
items.demo: On a sidepull, show the swing with right hand and right foot only, then stop it with a flag.

items.name: Dab
items.definition: Accidentally touching the ground, mat, spotter or a hold from another problem during a climb.
items.kid: A bump on the floor or a wrong hold by accident.
items.demo: On a low start, show how a heel brushing the mat counts as a dab.

items.name: Highball
items.definition: A tall boulder problem where a fall carries much higher risk.
items.kid: A really tall boulder.
items.demo: Compare the gym's tallest problem with the idea of one twice as high.

items.name: Hangdog
items.definition: Resting on the rope after a fall or take, then climbing on without going back to the ground.
items.kid: Hanging on the rope to rest, then keep going.
items.demo: Climber says take, rests, and continues.

items.name: Whipper
items.definition: A big lead fall, usually from well above the last clip.
items.kid: A long fall on lead.
items.demo: See Lead Fall Progression.

items.name: Runout
items.definition: The distance between clips (protection) on a lead route; a long runout means a longer potential fall.
items.kid: How far you climb above your last clip.
items.demo: Point at two bolts and estimate the fall from halfway between them.

items.name: Pogo
items.definition: A dynamic move where one leg swings to build momentum to reach a far hold.
items.kid: Swing a leg like a pendulum to boost up.
items.demo: Show a pogo to a jug on an easy low problem.

items.name: Bicycle
items.definition: On steep terrain, one foot pushes on a hold while the other toe-hooks under it, pinching the hold with the feet.
items.kid: One foot pushes, the other pulls, like bike pedals.
items.demo: On a low overhang volume, push with one toe and pull with the other.

items.name: Open-Hand Grip
items.definition: Gripping with fingers relaxed and joints not sharply bent; the recommended default grip for growing fingers.
items.kid: Hold on with soft, flat fingers, not curled tight.
items.demo: Compare open hand and half crimp on a big edge.

items.name: Half Crimp
items.definition: A grip on an edge with the middle finger joints bent about 90 degrees and the thumb off.
items.kid: Fingers bent like a little table on the edge.
items.demo: Show on a big edge; for younger kids, practise open hand first.

items.name: Bat Hang
items.definition: Hanging upside down from hooked or wedged feet to rest or reach.
items.kid: Hanging upside down from your feet like a bat.
items.demo: Show low with a spotter; see Heel Hook and Toe Hook.

items.name: Choss
items.definition: Loose, crumbly or rotten rock.
items.kid: Rock that is loose and crumbly.
items.demo: See Foot Notes (Look Out for Choss!).

items.name: Sewing-Machine Leg
items.definition: Involuntary shaking of a leg from fatigue, stress or fear.
items.kid: When your leg shakes because it's tired or nervous.
items.demo: Have a climber drop the heel and breathe out; watch the shake settle.

items.name: Sandbag
items.definition: A climb graded easier than it really is.
items.kid: A climb that is harder than its number says.
items.demo: After Guess the Grade, ask which climbs felt sandbagged.

items.name: Chimney
items.definition: A gap wide enough to fit the body, climbed by pressing back, feet and hands against opposite sides.
items.kid: Climbing up a gap by pushing on both sides.
items.demo: Show in a gym corner, starting from a stem.

items.name: Jamming
items.definition: Wedging a hand, finger or foot into a crack to hold on.
items.kid: Wedging your hand or foot into a crack.
items.demo: If the gym has a crack feature, show a hand jam low.

items.name: Stick Clip
items.definition: A long pole that clips a quickdraw and rope to the first bolt from the ground.
items.kid: A long pole to clip the first bolt from the ground.
items.demo: Show it before outdoor lead days.

items.name: Eye-to-Foot Contact
items.definition: Watching the foot all the way onto the hold so the toe lands on the best part of it.
items.kid: Watch your foot until it touches the hold.
items.demo: See Silent Feet and Sticky Feet.

items.name: Base of Support
items.definition: The area between the hands and feet holding the body; balance holds while the center of gravity stays over it.
items.kid: The shape your hands and feet make; keep your hips inside it.
items.demo: Stand on two footholds, then one, and feel balance change; see Plumb Line.

items.name: Weight Transfer
items.definition: Moving the body's weight from one foot to the other before or during a move.
items.kid: Shifting your weight onto one foot before moving the other.
items.demo: See Plumb Line.

items.name: Full Crimp
items.definition: A crimp with the thumb locked over or beside the index finger; the hardest grip on finger joints, so youth climbers favor open hand and half crimp.
items.kid: A crimp with your thumb locked on top; we use open hand instead.
items.demo: Show only to explain why we use open hand and half crimp.

items.name: Thumb Sprag
items.definition: Pressing the thumb against a feature opposite the fingers for extra grip.
items.kid: Using your thumb to push against the hold for extra grip.
items.demo: On an edge with a side, grip with and without the thumb.

items.name: Campusing
items.definition: Climbing with hands only and no feet; campus-board training is for experienced climbers about 16 and older.
items.kid: Climbing with no feet; campus boards wait until you're older.
items.demo: Mention only; see Peter Pans for older teens.

items.name: Hand-Foot Match
items.definition: Placing a foot on the same hold as a hand, often for a high step or when footholds are scarce.
items.kid: Putting your foot on the hold your hand is on.
items.demo: See Mantle Practice.

items.name: Walkthrough
items.definition: Crossing the moving foot past the weighted foot, between the body and the wall, onto the next hold.
items.kid: Stepping one foot past the other, close to the wall.
items.demo: See Furthest-Point Traverse.

items.name: Typewriter Match
items.definition: Matching a hold too small for both hands by swapping fingers off one at a time, like typing.
items.kid: Sharing a small hold by trading fingers.
items.demo: Match a narrow edge one finger at a time.

items.name: Fast Leg, Slow Foot
items.definition: Moving the leg quickly to the next position, then placing the foot slowly and precisely.
items.kid: Quick leg, careful toe.
items.demo: See Hover Feet.

items.name: Light Grip
items.definition: Holding on just hard enough not to slip; over-gripping wastes energy and pumps the forearms early.
items.kid: Holding on only as hard as you need to.
items.demo: See Tap Your Thumbs.

items.name: Pressing
items.definition: Flipping the hand palm-down to push the body in a direction; used in mantles, corners and long reaches.
items.kid: Pushing down on the wall with your palm.
items.demo: See Mantle Practice.

items.name: Rose Move
items.definition: A rare cross-under where the reaching arm passes under the locked-off arm, turning the body away from the wall.
items.kid: Reaching under your other arm and twisting around.
items.demo: Coach demo on a low traverse.

items.name: Twist Lock
items.definition: A move with the hips turned sideways to the wall and the pulling arm locked tight while the other hand reaches far.
items.kid: Turning sideways and pulling in tight to reach.
items.demo: See Pivot Practice.

items.name: Heel-Toe Cam
items.definition: Jamming the heel against one surface and the toe against another to hold the body on, often in a crack or under a roof.
items.kid: Wedging your heel and toe between two parts of the wall.
items.demo: Low roof or crack feature.

items.name: G-Tox
items.definition: A shake-out that alternates the free arm above the head and below the waist to help the forearm recover.
items.kid: Shaking out with your arm up high, then down low.
items.demo: See G-Tox Shake-Out.

items.name: Bolt
items.definition: A permanent anchor drilled into the rock, with a hanger for clipping a quickdraw on sport routes.
items.kid: A metal ring fixed in the rock for clipping the rope.
items.demo: Point out bolts on the lead wall.

items.name: Flapper
items.definition: A flap of torn skin, usually on a fingertip or palm, from friction on the holds.
items.kid: When a bit of skin tears open on your hand.
items.demo: Show how to tape and file skin.

items.name: Hangboard
items.definition: A board of edges and pockets for finger-strength hangs; deferred until about age 16 for youth climbers because of growth-plate risk.
items.kid: A board for training finger strength, saved for older teens.
items.demo: Explain why it waits until about 16.

items.name: Deliberate Practice
items.definition: Practice that targets a specific weakness, with full focus and feedback, rather than just climbing more.
items.kid: Practising one thing on purpose and checking how it went.
items.demo: Pick one skill to work on this session.

items.name: Process Goal
items.definition: A goal fully in the climber's control, about how they climb (read before each try, rest fully) rather than what they send.
items.kid: A goal about how you climb, not what you finish.
items.demo: See Today's Process Goal.

items.name: Outcome Goal
items.definition: A goal about a result, such as sending a certain climb or grade; useful long term but partly out of the climber's control on any given day.
items.kid: A goal about finishing a certain climb.
items.little: The climb I want to finish.
items.demo: Compare with a process goal in a goal-setting chat.

items.name: Microbeta
items.definition: The fine details of a sequence: exactly where on a hold to grab or stand, a small change in hip or foot angle.
items.kid: The tiny details of how to do a move.
items.demo: See One Change Per Try.

items.name: Flow
items.definition: Climbing continuously, linking moves with the hips so one movement carries into the next instead of stopping at every hold.
items.kid: Climbing smoothly without stopping.
items.demo: See Climb with Flow.

items.name: Tempo
items.definition: The speed and rhythm a climber moves at; good climbers change tempo, slowing on precise moves and speeding up where momentum helps.
items.kid: How fast or slow you climb.
items.demo: See Static and Dynamic or Climb to the Beat.

items.name: Momentum
items.definition: Using the body's motion, from a hip swing or leg push, to carry into the next hold instead of pulling statically.
items.kid: Using a swing or push to help you move.
items.demo: See Step-Up Springs.

items.name: Anti-Style
items.definition: The type of climbing a climber finds hardest or avoids, such as slab for a steep-wall climber; practising it builds an all-round climber.
items.kid: The kind of climbing you find hardest.
items.demo: Ask each climber to name theirs and pick one climb in that style.

items.name: System Board
items.definition: A steep training wall with a fixed grid or dense spread of holds used to set many problems; system boards often have matching holds on both sides. Mostly for older, trained climbers.
items.kid: A steep wall packed with holds for training.
items.demo: Point it out and explain who uses it and why.

items.name: Compression
items.definition: Holding on by squeezing two holds or features toward each other with the arms wide, like hugging a barrel, while the feet press and the core stays tight.
items.kid: Squeezing two holds toward each other like a big hug.
items.demo: See Squeeze Boulders.

items.name: Figure-Four
items.definition: An advanced move in which the climber hooks a leg over the opposite arm, which is on a good hold, and presses down with that leg to reach higher; rare indoors and more common in mixed climbing.
items.kid: Hooking your leg over your arm to reach higher.
items.demo: Coach-only demo on a big jug near the ground; not one for young kids to practise.

items.name: Lache
items.definition: A dynamic sideways move in which the climber builds momentum with the legs and hips, lets go with the hands and flies to a hold to the side.
items.kid: Letting go and flying sideways to the next hold.
items.demo: Show a video; older teens try it only low, over a clear mat, with a spotter.

items.name: Paddle Dyno
items.definition: A multi-move dyno in which the climber slaps one or more holds that can't be held, using each only to push on to the next, before grabbing a hold that can.
items.kid: Slapping one hold to bounce to the next.
items.demo: Coach demo for older teens; see Double-Hand Moves first.

items.name: Double Dyno
items.definition: A move in which both hands leave their holds and grab new ones at the same time, driven mostly by the legs.
items.kid: Moving both hands at once.
items.demo: See Double-Hand Moves.

items.name: Hand Traverse
items.definition: Moving sideways on the hands where there are no real footholds, so the feet smear or press on the wall.
items.kid: Moving sideways mostly on your hands.
items.demo: Show a few moves along a jug rail near the ground.

items.name: Ape Index
items.definition: A comparison of a climber's arm span with their height; a positive ape index means the arms span more than the climber is tall.
items.kid: How long your arms are compared with how tall you are.
items.demo: Measure arm span and height with a tape measure; it changes as kids grow.

items.name: Beta Break
items.definition: A sequence other than the one the setter intended, or other than the one usually used on a boulder.
items.kid: Finding a different way than the setter planned.
items.demo: See Wrong Beta Only.

items.name: Dialled
items.definition: Having a move or sequence learned so completely that it can be repeated reliably.
items.kid: When you know a climb so well you can do it every time.
items.demo: See Redpoint Tactics.

items.name: Link
items.definition: Climbing two or more sections of a route or boulder together without falling or resting, after working them separately.
items.kid: Joining parts of a climb together without stopping.
items.demo: See Redpoint Tactics.

items.name: Highpoint
items.definition: The highest hold a climber reaches on a climb before falling; on a project, a long link from the middle to the top often says more about progress than the highpoint from the ground.
items.kid: The highest place you got to on a climb.
items.demo: Mark each climber's own highpoint with a sticker and revisit it next week.

items.name: Topo
items.definition: A sketch or photo of a route or boulder with the line and main features marked.
items.kid: A map of a climb.
items.demo: See Draw the Route.

items.name: Crag
items.definition: A natural cliff or rock area with a number of sport or trad routes close together.
items.kid: A climbing cliff in nature.
items.demo: Show a photo of a local crag and compare it with the gym wall.

items.name: French Start
items.definition: Starting a boulder by using the floor to move to the second hold without first being established on the start holds; it doesn't count as a valid start under most event rules.
items.kid: Pushing off the floor instead of starting on the start holds.
items.demo: See Start Holds; show a proper start, then the floor push.

items.name: Ground Fall
items.definition: A fall in which the climber reaches the ground, for example on lead before enough clips are in, from too much slack, or when the belayer doesn't hold the rope; preventing it is a main reason for belay and clipping practice.
items.kid: A fall that reaches the ground.
items.demo: On the ground, show why the first clips and tidy slack matter on lead.

items.name: Live Rope
items.definition: In lead climbing, the part of the rope between the lead climber and the belayer.
items.kid: The rope between the leader and the belayer.
items.demo: Point to it during Ground Clipping Practice.

items.name: Sharp End
items.definition: The end of the rope tied to the lead climber; being on the sharp end means leading.
items.kid: Being the leader on the rope.
items.demo: Use the term during Mock Lead.

items.name: Belay Glasses
items.definition: Glasses with angled lenses that let the belayer watch the climber without tipping the head back, reducing neck strain.
items.kid: Glasses that let a belayer look up without bending their neck.
items.demo: Let teen belayers try a pair on the ground.

items.name: Cue Word
items.definition: A short word or phrase a climber says to focus on the movement they need most, such as ‘quiet feet’, before or between tries.
items.kid: A word you say to remind yourself what to focus on.
items.demo: See Pre-Climb Routine.

items.name: Rail
items.definition: A long horizontal hold or edge that runs across the wall, which can be gripped anywhere along its length and often shuffled along.
items.kid: A long sideways hold you can slide your hands along.
items.demo: Shuffle both hands along a rail on a low traverse.

items.name: Ledge
items.definition: A flat horizontal shelf on the wall or a boulder, big enough to stand on or press down on; often where a mantle happens.
items.kid: A flat shelf on the wall.
items.demo: See Mantle Practice.

items.name: Scum
items.definition: Pressing a part of the body other than the hands or sole of the shoe (the top of the toe, the knee, thigh or hip) against the wall or a feature for extra friction or support; a knee bar is the best-known scum.
items.kid: Pushing your knee, hip or the top of your toe on the wall to help you stick.
items.demo: Press the top of the toe against a volume while reaching; see Cam and Knee-Bar Rests.

items.name: Smedge
items.definition: A mix of a smear and an edge: pressing the shoe rubber onto a tiny edge or rough patch that is too small to stand on with the edge alone.
items.kid: Half standing on a tiny bump, half smearing.
items.demo: Stand on a small foot chip with the heel low and the rubber pressed in.

items.name: Pendulum
items.definition: The sideways swing a top-roped or lead climber takes when they fall while off to the side of the anchor or last clip; plan for it and keep the swing path clear.
items.kid: Swinging sideways like a pendulum when you fall off to the side.
items.demo: On top rope, show where a climber off to the side would swing; see Top-Rope Fall Practice.

items.name: Fall Line
items.definition: The path a falling climber (or a dropped object) will follow; belayers, spotters and waiting climbers stay clear of another climber's fall line.
items.kid: The line you would fall along if you let go.
items.demo: Show the fall line under a climber before anyone walks underneath; see Fall Zones Tour.

items.name: Rope Drag
items.definition: Friction that makes the rope hard to pull up while leading, caused by the rope bending through quickdraws that zigzag or by the rope running over an edge.
items.kid: When the rope feels heavy and stuck because it bends through the clips.
items.demo: On a mock lead, clip zigzag draws and feel the extra pull.

items.name: Clipping
items.definition: Putting the rope into a quickdraw while leading (or attaching to an anchor); a climber may call “Clipping!” so the belayer gives slack quickly.
items.kid: Putting the rope into a quickdraw.
items.demo: See Ground Clipping Practice.

items.name: Knee Pad
items.definition: A sleeve worn on the leg just above the knee, usually with a sticky rubber or neoprene layer, that makes knee bars grip better and protects the skin.
items.kid: A sticky sleeve on your leg that helps knee bars stick.
items.demo: Try the same knee bar with and without a pad.

items.name: Chalk Ball
items.definition: A fabric ball filled with chalk that is squeezed onto the hands; it makes less dust than loose chalk.
items.kid: A little bag ball of chalk you squeeze.
items.demo: Squeeze the ball in the chalk bag, then rub hands together.

items.name: Circuit
items.definition: A set of boulder problems at a similar level, often marked with one color or label, meant to be climbed one after another.
items.kid: A group of climbs at the same level you do in a row.
items.demo: See Arch Circuit or Power Endurance Circuits.

items.name: Lap
items.definition: One more climb of the same route or problem, usually an easy one, done for practice, warm-up or endurance.
items.kid: Climbing the same climb again.
items.demo: See Easy Continuous Laps.

items.name: Open Hip
items.definition: A hip position where the pelvis turns away from the wall so the outside of the hip and the outside edge of the shoe face the wall; common when back-stepping or reaching sideways.
items.kid: Turning your hip out so the side of your body faces the wall.
items.little: Turn your tummy a little sideways.
items.demo: On a vertical wall, back-step a foothold and show the open hip next to square hips.

items.name: Closed Hip
items.definition: A hip position with the pelvis square (or nearly square) to the wall and the inside edges of both shoes facing in; the default “frontstep” stance on vertical ground.
items.kid: Hips facing the wall, both feet using the inside edges.
items.demo: See Frontstep; contrast with Open Hip on the same two footholds.

items.name: Coordination Move
items.definition: A modern boulder move where hands and feet must move together in a timed pattern (for example a skate/step-through into a throw, or a jump into a foot stab); fails if one part is late.
items.kid: A move where your hands and feet have to move at the same time in a pattern.
items.demo: See Build-the-Move Lab (skate / jump-to-foot-stab patterns) on easy holds.

items.name: Volume Press
items.definition: Turning a pulling move on a volume into a press (pushing down or out with the hands) to stand or mantle onto it; often a one- or two-handed transition on competition-style volumes.
items.kid: Pulling on a big shape, then pushing down to stand up on it.
items.demo: On a low volume, pull to the lip then press the palms and stand; see Mantle Practice.

items.name: Frog Position
items.definition: Both knees turned outward with hips close to the wall so the arms can stay straighter on steep ground; a Neil Gresham teaching shape for keeping tension without a drop-knee.
items.kid: Both knees pointed out like a frog so you can keep straight arms.
items.demo: On an easy overhang, turn both knees out, hips in, arms long; contrast with a drop-knee on one side.

items.name: Pinkpoint
items.definition: Leading a route with the quickdraws already clipped (or pre-placed), as opposed to a clean redpoint where the climber places the draws on the lead; used in training and some outdoor contexts.
items.kid: Leading with the clips already on the bolts.
items.demo: On a mock lead, contrast placing draws and climbing with draws pre-hung; see Ground Clipping Practice.

items.name: X-Motion
items.definition: Balanced movement pattern that anchors the body from one hand to the opposite foot so the free hand can move with less effort; climbers link a series of these half-X anchors while ascending.
items.kid: Left hand to right foot, then right hand to left foot.
items.little: Opposite hand and foot stick together.
items.demo: See X-Motion Laps; freeze with left hand and right foot weighted, free right hand hovering, then switch.

items.name: Rooting
items.definition: Placing a foot on a hold and actively pulling the hips toward that foot with the glutes, hamstrings and lower back, rather than only pressing or flagging.
items.kid: Your foot pulls your hips in toward it.
items.demo: See Rooting Drill; on a sideways move, root a high foot and bring the hip in before the hand reaches.

items.name: Same-Side Climbing
items.definition: Climbing while weighted primarily on one side of the body (same-side hand and foot), which often invites a barn door unless timed dynamically, reverse-flagged or hip-shifted.
items.kid: Both anchors on the same side of your body.
items.little: Same-side hand and foot—watch for the door swing.
items.demo: Freeze on right hand and right foot only, show the peel, then fix with a reverse flag or a quick deadpoint catch.

items.name: 4-4-4 Breathing
items.definition: Simple arousal-control breath: inhale for 4 counts, hold for 4, exhale for 4; used before a try or a committing move.
items.kid: Breathe in for 4, hold for 4, out for 4.
items.little: Slow balloon breaths: in, hold, out.
items.demo: Whole group practices one round on the ground, then one round before a warm-up climb; see Belly Breathing.

items.name: Thoracic Spine
items.definition: The middle section of the spine behind the ribs. Good rotation here helps climbers reach behind them, stem in corners and turn into drop knees without straining the shoulders or lower back.
items.kid: Your mid-back, the part that twists when you reach behind you.
items.little: The part of your back that turns like a door.
items.demo: Lie on your side and open one arm like a book; feel the twist in the mid-back, not the hips. See Open Book Twists.

items.name: Serratus Anterior
items.definition: A muscle along the ribs that holds the shoulder blade flat against the ribcage; it helps steady the shoulder when reaching overhead.
items.kid: A muscle on your side ribs that keeps your shoulder blade steady when you reach up.
items.little: The muscle that keeps your shoulder blade snug.
items.demo: Do one push-up plus and feel the shoulder blades spread at the top. See Push-Up Plus.

items.name: Adductors
items.definition: The muscles on the inner thigh. Climbers use them for drop knees, wide stems and high feet, and they are rarely stretched.
items.kid: Your inner-thigh muscles that pull the legs together and help with stems and drop knees.
items.little: The muscles that help you do the splits.
items.demo: Sit in a butterfly stretch and notice where you feel it. See Butterfly Stretch.

items.name: Controlled Articular Rotations
items.definition: Very slow, biggest-possible circles of a single joint, done while the rest of the body stays still, to keep and find range of motion.
items.kid: Drawing the biggest slow circle you can with one joint while the rest of you stays still.
items.little: Super-slow giant circles with your arm.
items.demo: Make one 10-second shoulder circle with a tight fist and a still body. See Slow Shoulder Circles.

items.name: Retraction Test
items.definition: Pulling auto-belay webbing out and letting it rewind to confirm the device is taking in line before you clip and climb.
items.kid: Pull the auto-belay strap down and let it zip back so you feel a tug.
items.little: Pull, let go, feel the tug.
items.demo: Coach pulls webbing, releases, everyone says “tug!” then kids try under staff eyes.

items.name: Double Check
items.definition: ABC-endorsed habit on auto belays: a visual harness self-check plus a physical retraction test before leaving the ground, every single climb.
items.kid: Check your harness and feel the auto-belay tug every time, even if you just climbed.
items.demo: Poster walk + practise the two-part check at the flag.

items.name: Belay Flag
items.definition: A highly visible barrier at the base of an auto-belay lane that blocks starting the climb until the climber has clipped in; follow the gym’s flag-up / flag-down markings.
items.kid: The big marker you move only after you are clipped in.
items.little: The stop sign at the wall.
items.demo: Show flag up and down and have kids mime clip-then-move-flag.

items.name: Auto-Belay Lane
items.definition: The marked vertical corridor an auto-belay protects. Climbing outside it, beside the device, or above the device leaves you unprotected by that device.
items.kid: Stay inside the painted or taped lane under your auto belay.
items.demo: Walk the lane edges on the floor before climbing.

items.name: Auto-Belay Webbing
items.definition: The strap that feeds from an auto-belay unit to the climber’s carabiner; it must retract as you climb and lower you when you sit back.
items.kid: The strap from the machine to your harness clip.
items.demo: Point to webbing, carabiner, and device as three linked parts.

items.name: Triple-Action Carabiner
items.definition: A self-locking carabiner that needs three motions to open (often slide, twist, then gate). Common on auto-belay connection points.
items.kid: A clip that takes three moves to open so it stays locked while you climb.
items.demo: Slowly open and close one on the ground; never toss it so the webbing retracts uncontrolled.

items.name: Tri-Axial Loading
items.definition: Loading a carabiner in three directions at once (for example clipping an auto-belay into both harness hard points). Carabiners are built for two-direction loading along the spine.
items.kid: When a clip gets pulled three ways at once—something we avoid by clipping only the belay loop.
items.demo: Show belay-loop clip and two hard points with a diagram or coach demo on the ground.

items.name: Clipping Stance
items.definition: A balanced body position with secure feet and at least one solid hand so the other hand can clip without barn-dooring or lunging.
items.kid: Get your feet and one hand solid before you clip.
items.demo: On a board, try clipping while stretched and from a solid stance; compare.

items.name: Short-Roping
items.definition: Belaying with so little slack that the climber is tugged off balance or cannot move freely—especially disruptive when a leader needs slack to clip.
items.kid: When the belayer holds the rope too tight and pulls the climber off their holds.
items.demo: Ground walk: belayer keeps rope slightly soft and yanking the partner.

items.name: Assisted Braking Device
items.definition: A belay device that helps pinch or cam the rope under load. Still requires a brake hand and gym-specific technique.
items.kid: A belay tool that helps grab the rope in a fall, but your brake hand still works the whole time.
items.demo: Show brake position on the gym’s ABD and a tube device; staff teach device specifics.

items.name: Tube Device
items.definition: A friction belay device without assisted braking cams; the belayer’s brake-hand technique (often PBUS) creates the holding power.
items.kid: A belay tool where your brake hand and body position do all the holding work.
items.demo: Thread rope, show brake position below the device.

items.name: Gate Orientation
items.definition: Which way a quickdraw’s carabiner gates face when hung. Gates are usually oriented to reduce the chance of a rope or feature pressing them open during a fall or movement.
items.kid: Which way the clip’s door faces when you hang a draw.
items.demo: Hang two draws with opposite gate directions and explain the gym’s preferred pattern.

items.name: Carabiner Spine
items.definition: The solid back side of a carabiner opposite the gate; the strongest loading path runs along the spine.
items.kid: The strong back of the clip, opposite the door.
items.demo: Point spine and gate on a large demo biner.

items.name: Dogbone
items.definition: The sewn sling that joins the two carabiners of a quickdraw.
items.kid: The strong strap in the middle of a quickdraw.
items.demo: Disassemble a practice draw into two biners + dogbone.

items.name: Mock-Lead Method
items.definition: Practising lead clipping and rope awareness while a top rope or auto belay is the true belay that would catch a fall.
items.kid: Pretend lead: you clip draws, but another rope or auto belay is really holding you.
items.little: Practice lead with a helper rope.
items.demo: Show the backup rope and the practice lead rope before leaving the ground.

items.name: Pre-Hung Draws
items.definition: Quickdraws already clipped to the bolts before the climber starts, so the leader only clips the rope. Related outdoor term: pinkpoint.
items.kid: The clips are already on the bolts; you only put the rope in.
items.demo: Contrast a bare bolt hanger with a pre-hung draw.

items.name: Fall Factor
items.definition: A way of describing fall severity: roughly fall length divided by the length of rope out. Higher factors mean a sharper catch for the same climber and belayer skill.
items.kid: A number idea: falling far on only a little rope out feels harsher than falling the same distance on lots of rope out.
items.little: Short rope out plus a long fall means a bigger jolt.
items.demo: Whiteboard sticks: 1 m fall on 2 m of rope and 1 m fall on 10 m of rope.

items.name: Belay Stance
items.definition: How the belayer stands and braces—usually facing the wall, ready to move—so they can take in, pay out, and catch without being pulled off balance.
items.kid: The strong standing position a belayer uses so a catch does not yank them over.
items.demo: Compare a casual stance with an athletic braced stance on a ground tug.

items.name: Paying Out
items.definition: Feeding rope to the climber so they can move up or clip without being short-roped.
items.kid: Giving the climber more rope on purpose.
items.demo: Partner walks away while belayer feeds smooth slack.

items.name: Taking In
items.definition: Pulling rope through the belay device to remove slack as the climber moves up or sits.
items.kid: Pulling the extra rope in so it stays tidy.
items.demo: Partner walks toward belayer; belayer takes in without losing the brake hand.

items.name: Brake Position
items.definition: The hand and rope position that maximizes friction in the device—typically the brake strand held firmly below a tube device. The brake hand stays on the brake strand.
items.kid: Where your never-let-go hand holds the rope to lock the device.
items.demo: Freeze mid-PBUS and check every brake hand.

items.name: Backup Belayer
items.definition: A second person ready to grab the brake strand and support the primary belayer, used while learning and often kept in youth classes even after some climbers certify.
items.kid: A helper who stands ready to grab the brake rope if needed.
items.demo: Triangle roles: climber, belayer, backup.

items.name: Lead Certification
items.definition: Gym-specific assessment that grants permission to lead climb and/or lead belay indoors. Often requires minimum age, top-rope belay competence, and a practical test.
items.kid: The gym test you pass before you may lead on your own.
items.demo: Read the gym’s rubric aloud; map class drills to each line.

items.name: Clipping Call
items.definition: A lead climber’s call that they are about to clip, cueing the belayer to pay out enough slack quickly without flooding the system.
items.kid: Saying “clipping” so your belayer gives you rope for the clip.
items.demo: Call-and-response on the ground: “Clipping!” then smooth payout.

items.name: Hard Catch
items.definition: A sudden catch with little give. Sometimes appropriate near the ground; can feel harsh and increase force on higher falls. Contrast with a soft catch (already in the library).
items.kid: A sudden stop with almost no give.
items.demo: Contrast with soft-catch concepts in Soft-Catch Concept Lab; coach names when each is used.

items.name: First Clip
items.definition: The first quickdraw a leader clips. Until it and the next clips are in, ground-fall risk is highest, so many gyms teach stick-clipping or extra care here.
items.kid: Your very first clip on lead—take extra care.
items.demo: Stand under bolt one and talk through options (stick clip, solid stance, coach belay).

items.name: Rope Direction
items.definition: How the rope should run through a quickdraw’s rope-end carabiner so a fall loads it without levering the gate; the opposite error is a back-clip.
items.kid: Putting the rope through the draw the right way so it cannot pop out easily.
items.little: Rope the right way in the clip.
items.demo: Back-Clip Spotting Board activity.

items.name: Lead Belay
items.definition: Belaying a climber who is clipping overhead protection. Requires smooth payout, fast take-in, active stance, and gym lead-belay certification.
items.kid: Holding the rope for someone who is clipping on the way up.
items.demo: Ground payout/take-in, then watch a coach demo on a real lead with a backup.

items.name: Top-Rope Belay
items.definition: Belaying when the rope already runs through an anchor above the climber, so falls are short and the belayer mainly takes in slack and lowers.
items.kid: Belaying when the rope is already through the top.
items.demo: Trace climber to anchor to belayer path with a finger.

items.name: Partner-Check List
items.definition: The spoken sequence of items two climbers verify before every climb: harness, knot, device, locker, rope end, and extras for lead.
items.kid: The checklist you say out loud with your buddy before climbing.
items.demo: Point-trace through a real pair before they leave the ground.

items.name: Auto-Belay Induction
items.definition: Staff-delivered, hands-on teaching of harness fit, clipping, retraction test, lowering, lane rules, and the risk of climbing unclipped before a climber may use auto belays unsupervised.
items.kid: The staff lesson you must finish before using auto belays by yourself.
items.demo: Run the induction steps as a class block even for kids who will remain coach-clipped.

items.name: Complacency Trap
items.definition: The pattern ABC highlights where skilled climbers skip the clip-in routine out of habit after many successful climbs—the leading human-error theme in auto-belay incidents.
items.kid: Getting so used to auto belays that you forget to clip—exactly why we double-check every time.
items.demo: Tell the ABC story in age-fit words, then redo a slow double-check.

items.name: Lowering Path
items.definition: The clear space a climber needs beneath and around them before sitting back to lower on rope or auto belay.
items.kid: Looking down to make sure nobody is under you before you lower.
items.demo: Climber points to three clear spots before calling lower.

items.name: Dynamic Rope Stretch
items.definition: The designed stretch in a climbing rope that absorbs fall energy. It is why catches feel springy and why belayers still need careful slack management.
items.kid: Climbing ropes stretch on purpose so a fall softens a little.
items.demo: Two climbers gently pull a flaked rope on the ground to feel stretch—no bouncing people.

items.name: Planned Practice Fall
items.definition: A fall the climber and belayer intentionally set up for learning, with terrain, height, and belay style agreed beforehand—not an unexpected slip.
items.kid: A fall you both plan on purpose to learn from, with a coach’s plan.
items.demo: Agree height and words before Push-Off Fall Practice.

items.name: Comfort-Zone Edge
items.definition: The difficulty of fall practice a climber can do while staying mostly relaxed. Coaches advance only when body language stays calm at the current edge.
items.kid: The hardest practice fall that still feels okay enough to repeat.
items.demo: After a set, ask “could you gladly do that again?” before progressing.

items.name: Closed Belay System
items.definition: A belay setup that includes a stopper knot or other end method so the rope cannot run completely through the device.
items.kid: Tying the rope end so it cannot slip all the way through the belay tool.
items.demo: Closed-System Rope End activity.

items.name: Ground-Fall Zone
items.definition: The portion of a lead near the start where a fall may still reach the floor because not enough clips are in or slack is mismanaged.
items.kid: The low part of a lead where a fall might still hit the floor.
items.demo: Stand at bolts 1–3 and mark with tape where a fall might deck if unclipped.

items.name: Retraction Speed
items.definition: How quickly an auto belay reels in webbing. Climbers must not climb faster than this rate or a slack loop appears.
items.kid: How fast the auto belay pulls the strap in—you climb only as fast as it can keep up.
items.demo: Show a slack loop on purpose at ground level (coach), then reset and climb slower.

items.name: Belay-Loop Only Clip
items.definition: The rule that an auto-belay carabiner clips to the harness belay loop alone, not through both tie-in hard points, to avoid tri-axial loading.
items.kid: Clip the auto belay to the strong front loop only.
items.demo: Harness Parts Callout, then a correct and incorrect clip demo on the ground.
